final_message:
Done. All three versions are complete and verified.

## Algorithm (shared by all three)

One pass over the lowercased input. Words are maximal letter runs; a pair `(word_i, word_{i+1})` is counted only when no `.`, `!` or `?` lies between them. Then totals are emitted plus the top-20 pairs, sorted by count descending with ties broken by first/second word byte order. Distinct words are ~35k and distinct pairs ~6.5M at benchmark scale (60 MB, 7M words).

## Version notes

**`rust/src/main.rs`** (~3.5 s on 60 MB) — hand-rolled for cache efficiency: file read + in-place ASCII lowercase; a 256-entry byte-class table drives a single scan; words interned into sequential ids via a custom open-addressing table (hash + byte-compare, slots preallocated, rehash on growth); pairs counted in an open-addressing `u64 → u32` table keyed by `id1<<32|id2`; top-20 via `select_nth_unstable_by` + sort of the prefix with a byte-wise comparator; manual itoa + BufWriter output. `lto="fat"`, `codegen-units=1`, `panic="abort"`.

**`plain.py`** (~10.8 s) — stdlib only, pushes all heavy work into C: one `bytes.translate` maps `A-Z`→lowercase, `.!?`→`\n`, everything else→space, so `t.split(b"\n")` yields sentences and `s.split()` yields words exactly per spec; pair counting is a single global `Counter` fed `update(zip(ws, islice(ws, 1, None)))` (the C `_count_elements` loop). Top-20 avoids a full sort: `heapq.nlargest(20, counts)` gives the threshold count, then only pairs with `count >= threshold` are collected and sorted.

**`fast.py`** (~9 s) — NumPy throughout: vectorized letter/sentence masks give word spans; sentence membership via `searchsorted` over sentence-end positions. Words are encoded **exactly** (no hash-collision risk) as their base-256 little-endian value split into 64-bit limbs, built with per-byte gathers restricted to the shrinking subset of words long enough to have that byte, packed through an odd multiplier (a bijection mod 2⁶⁴) so words ≤16 bytes become one `uint64`; longer words fall back to a structured multi-field key. Word ids come from one `argsort` + boundary scatter; pair keys `id1*n_words+id2` (exact bijection) are counted with `np.unique(..., return_counts=True)`; top-20 via `np.partition` threshold + `np.lexsort` over (count, lex-rank of first word, lex-rank of second word).

## Verification

- **Samples**: s1, s2, s3 — **all three versions pass all three**.
- **Edge cases** (validated against an independent regex-based brute-force reference, all 3 versions × 8 cases): empty file, punctuation-only, single word, no sentence terminator (final-sentence rule), case folding, digits/quotes between words, and 17–31-letter words (exercises fast.py's multi-limb path). Two bugs this exposed were fixed: plain.py's small-distinct branch was unsorted, and fast.py crashed on zero-word input and on structured keys.
- **60 MB benchmark input** (7.0M words, 40k vocab): all three produce byte-identical output. Timings on this (noisy, concurrently loaded) machine: Rust ~3.5 s, fast.py ~9–11 s, plain.py ~10.8 s — machine load varied ±20% between runs.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
